statement: Lines parallel to the sides cut an equilateral triangle of side 4 into 16 small equilateral triangles of side 1. A beetle walks from small triangle to small triangle, each step crossing a shared side, and never enters a small triangle twice. What is the largest number of small triangles it can visit, including its starting one?

choices.misconception: I made the beetle walk along just the bottom row, which has 7 small triangles.
I saw that the route alternates between upward and downward triangles but did not let it start and finish on upward ones.
I noticed only that the three corner triangles, each with a single neighbour, cannot all be visited, and left out just one.
I thought a clever enough route could visit every small triangle.

hints: Small triangles point either up or down. Which kinds can be neighbours?
Use a colouring argument: every step goes between an upward and a downward triangle, so the route alternates. Count each kind, and the smaller count limits the length of the route.
There are 10 upward small triangles and only 6 downward ones.

solutions.reliable: The rows of small triangles contain 1, 3, 5 and 7 triangles, so 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 point up and 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 point down. Two small triangles sharing a side always point in opposite directions, so the route alternates up, down, up, down. With only 6 downward triangles available, the route has at most 6 downward and 7 upward triangles, so at most 13 in all. Thirteen is possible: start in the bottom left corner and walk right through 6 triangles of the bottom row, step up and walk left through 4 triangles, step up and walk right through 2, then step into the top triangle. The transferable idea: when every move switches between two kinds of cell, the scarcer kind limits the route.

whyOnTest: Sorting the triangles into up and down turns a fiddly search into a one-line bound, while trial routes suggest misleading answers.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
